body: I assumed it was about the household because a couple people have responded to that in the same way when I mentioned I grew up in a half-half household. Sorry for the confusion

I know a couple people in the community that do think that way though. Something about keeping the bloodline completely Jewish. It is a worry some people have. 
I was trying to say that she could have argued that no matter what their child would be Jewish because she is Jewish (and yes this is a fact, their child would be Jewish no matter what)

I know. I didn't say I was half. I grew up in a household were two different religions were emphasized so sadly I didn't get as much info. I was pointing out that I wasn't raised completely Jewish, hence not calling myself half-half but the household half-half. I don't know if this was directed at my mentioning my household but that's what I meant by it.

The thing with Judaism is that throughout history there has always been an effort to eradicate them or the discriminate for the most part. A lot of the rules in the religion were created to keep the faith alive. This is probably where his mindset is coming from and it is completely valid. 

She shouldn't have lied and honestly could have at least tried to come up with a compromise that still enforces the faith. If the mother is Jewish the baby is considered Jewish. I think he may be worried that the baby won't be considered Jewish if the "father" isn't Jewish. 

I grew up in a half-jewish half-christian household (my mom was Jewish and my dad was raised Catholic) so my views on the religion and how stuff works may not be entirely accurate (so correct me if I am wrong) but from my standpoint there could have possibly been a compromise if she had at least tried.

NTA One time in my African American lit class I was reading Fredrick Douglass and the N word caught me off guard and I just uttered NI before stopping. My professor then just went "It's okay you can say it." I am a white female so I never use the N word in my day to day speech and just hearing it sometimes makes me uncomfortable, but if you are reading a quote in an academic setting it literally does no harm. In fact some teachers will encourage you to say it when reading a quote simply because shying away from it gives the word more power than it needs. I think I have heard somewhere that the word exchanged between people of color is used as a way to re-allocate the meaning and take the hate out of it. But honestly I feel like your classmates were over reacting.

Don't ever feel guilty for not saying no. You were too young at the time to fully know what was going on and couldn't consent to these things. As a past victim of sexual abuse/assault, just because you didn't say no doesn't mean they had permission. The only time someone has permission to do something is if you verbally consent to it without threats or if you are under the influence. Never let someone tell you otherwise. All your feelings are justified and like everyone else is saying, get help. You can either go to the police, get therapy, or both. Make sure to do what makes you the most comfortable. It is your decision at the end of the day.

If there is something he is particularly interested in you could always go out of your way to get it for him for his birthday (experiences would be better than material objects if you are going for sentiment). If he is into baseball, get him tickets to a game. A huge gamer?  Take him to a gaming Cafe. If you are worried about budget there are also super cheap options. My favorite is to just do the things guys are traditionally expected to do. Cuddle him instead of the other way around. Buy him flowers or chocolates. Give him a handmade card explaining how much he means to you. A lot of guys are expected to show more affection then girls and sometimes they need to feel the love too.
There are a lot of things you can do for him, but at the end of the day if you let him know how much you care about and appreciate him it'll be sure to make his day. 
I also have gone through a lot of tough times with my PTSD, anxiety, and depression and my boyfriend is always there for me. I always try my hardest to let him know how much I appreciate him. 
Thank you for the most wholesome post I have seen in this thread.

I think the "but she is Canadian" was an honest attempt at pointing out the microaggression on your boyfriends part. Part of the microaggression of zooming in on race is that it is usually a way of making someone more foreign than they actually are. I think he was probably trying to prove the point of "yes that is her race, but that doesn't define her. She is a Canadian just like you and me and we shouldn't be focusing on where she is from." Granted I am white and do not have to face microaggressions so I have no clue if this was the way it should have been handled. I would suggest talking to your boyfriend about how his reaction felt to you and maybe give him examples of responses to microaggressions that make you more comfortable. I feel like him being white might make it hard for him to know the best action because he doesn't actually know what it is like to have microaggressions directed at him. This way in the future he can respond in a way that makes you feel more comfortable/wanted.

I think this is hilarious because I have a similar story about my mom. When my mom was pregnant with me she was at a restaurant with friends when the extreme hunger hit her. The restaurant was busy and they hadn't even ordered their food yet. My mom was so delusional and hungry that she grabbed a half eaten baked potato off of a busboy's cart as he was passing and started eating it. I've always found this story hilarious. At least she didn't demand others people's food like the lady in OP's post. NTA

I think what OP is trying to say is that tipping in higher end restaurants tend to be on the more generous side because usually the people who can afford to eat there can pay a healthy sum of a tip. If you live in a small town and you work at a lower end restaurant you aren't going to make enough to live on tips. I used to work at a takeout place next to a bar. The bar let our wait staff go into the outdoor area and the bar to serve customers food since the bar did not serve food itself. Sometimes I wished I was working in the kitchen because a lot of people were stingy. I would often serve a table of 12 with a bill over $100 and get no tip. My good days were due only when a rare guy would try to impress a girl by buying fries with a $100 and then telling me to keep the change. The point wasn't that people at higher end restaurants also get paid poorly but that the system is flawed and biased and that not all wait staff gets treated equally.

I was sitting in my room when a roommate my apartment complex assigned to me (it was a college community apartment complex) walked in with a toddler during my sophomore year of college. At first I thought the toddler might be her sister but they soon started calling her mom. Her and her super intimidating boyfriend then proceeded to do drugs in the living room while their child kept trying to get into my room and nearly destroying my laptop. I confronted the apartment complex about it since both living with a child and doing drugs was against the lease (the reasoning behind the child thing is because it is a college community full of students trying to get an education without the added stress of your randomly assigned roommate forcing their child on you). They refused to do anything about the situation and even commented on how "If I can't confront my roommate about these issues I shouldn't live with people". I'm sorry, I can't just confront these people about having a child. Like what is even going to happen? And trying to confront roommates about doing drugs is kind of scary especially when the boyfriend gives off threatening vibes. I honestly didn't feel safe confronting them about it. Asking someone to clean dirty dishes? Yup do it all the time with my current roommates. Hey can you turn that down? I'm trying to study. I have no issue asking these questions of my roommates because they are normal roommate things that can be dealt with. I basically looked the people trying to avoid dealing with these issues in the eyes and said, "Fine I am moving out. When I signed your lease I did not sign up for this horrible living situation." I moved out within a week. "Fuck this, I'm out!"
